newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico returns to Samurai market with tight spread.
newsitem.headline: Mexico returns to Samurai market with tight spread.

text.p: Mexico returned to the Samurai market on Thursday, placing a 50 billion yen seven-year bond that drew Japanese investors wanting decent yields and a reasonably good credit risk.

The United Mexican States (UMS), the federal government, said the bond had a coupon of 4.0 percent, or 219 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, well below its other recent issues in that market. Daiwa Securities led the issue.
"They found attractive pricing," Daiwa Securities chief representative officer Guillermo Anaya told Reuters.

"Investors are looking for more attractive returns, without taking too much of a risk, and Mexico is a case that combines the two. It is perceived as a good credit and offers better returns than many other Japanese instruments," he said.
The issue was taken up mainly by institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurance companies and regional banks.
The bond, worth about $400 million, fits in with Mexico's strategy of placing more bonds in non-dollar markets.

"By placing this issue we are taking advantage of the favourable financial conditions that are being offered right now in the Samurai market compared to other markets," the Finance Ministry said in a statement.

The last time Mexico made a trip to the Samurai market was in September last year, when it launched a six-year 70 billion yen issue with a yield of 5.0 percent, or 326 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
In June, Mexico issued a 10-year 100 billion yen bond with a yield of 6.75 percent, or 410 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Before that, last March the federal government placed a six-year 40 billion yen issue with a yield of 6.0 percent, or 390 basis points over similar U.S. Treasuries.
"If you compare it (the latest issue) with the other issues that Mexico has placed, they have improved their conditions," Anaya said.
The Finance Ministry added that Mexico was consolidating its presence in the Japanese market.
It said funds from the placement would be used to refinance short-term obligations.

Mexico has 43 billion yen worth of paper coming due in 1997 that was placed in 1995. Of that, 30 billion is from a 15-month note placed in December 1995. Also coming due is 13 billion yen of a two-year note that was also placed last December.

Analysts say that among other Mexican borrowers who could possibly go to the Samurai market sometime soon are state-owned oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex), and state development banks, Bancomext and Nafinsa.
